event: Battle of Adrianople — Emperor Valens killed by the Visigoths. The Roman army's worst defeat in centuries. The empire will never fully recover.
Death of Theodosius I — the Roman Empire permanently splits into Eastern and Western halves. The West begins its final decline.
Battle of Pollentia — Stilicho defeats Alaric's Visigoths in northern Italia, temporarily saving the Western Empire.
Crossing of the Rhine — Vandals, Alans, and Suebi flood into Gaul on the last day of the year. The Rhine frontier collapses permanently.
Execution of Stilicho — Emperor Honorius murders his best general on suspicion of treason. Thousands of barbarian soldiers in Roman service defect to Alaric.
Sack of Rome — Alaric's Visigoths sack Rome for three days. First time the city has fallen in 800 years. Shockwaves across the empire.
Emperor Honorius tells the cities of Britain to look to their own defense. Rome abandons the province. The legions will not return.
Visigoths settled in Aquitaine by the Roman government — given land in exchange for military service. A barbarian kingdom now exists inside the empire.
Vandals cross the Strait of Gibraltar to North Africa under King Gaiseric. Rome's grain supply is now under direct threat.
Vandals capture Carthage — Rome loses its primary grain source. The Western Empire's food supply is now controlled by a hostile power.
Battle of the Catalaunian Plains — Romans under Aetius and Visigoths together defeat Attila the Hun. The last great Roman military victory.
Attila invades Italia — destroys Aquileia, threatens Rome itself. Pope Leo I negotiates his withdrawal. The north is devastated.
Sack of Rome by the Vandals — worse than Alaric's sack in 410. Gaiseric's forces strip the city systematically for fourteen days.
Fall of the Western Roman Empire — the Germanic chieftain Odoacer deposes the last Western Emperor, Romulus Augustulus. The empire is over.
Grain shipments from Africa grow irregular. Prices in Italian markets rise as supply becomes uncertain. Merchants hoard what they can.
After the sack of Rome, famine grips the city. Refugees flood north toward Ravenna and Ariminum, straining local food supplies.
Trade along the Via Flaminia slows as barbarian raids make overland travel dangerous. Merchants in Ariminum report fewer ships arriving each month.
With Carthage in Vandal hands, the African grain supply to Italia is cut off. Bread prices triple. The poor go hungry.
Augustine of Hippo begins writing The City of God in response to pagans who blame the sack of Rome on the Christian god replacing the old ones.
Augustine dies as the Vandals besiege Hippo Regius. His writings will define Western Christianity for a thousand years.
Plague recurs in the crowded quarters of Ravenna as the imperial court relocates there. Sickness follows wherever the refugees gather.
